name: Vandevert Ranch
label: Vandevert Ranch
about_prose: What was here before the gated community? A working cattle ranch, for the better part of a century. William Plutarch Vandevert homesteaded on the Little Deschutes River in 1892, on land that predates both the city of Bend and Deschutes County itself. The ranch sits about 15 miles south of Bend and roughly 2 miles from Sunriver, its elevation running from 4,160 feet near the river to 4,180 feet at the entrance gate. Vandevert was born in 1854 near Cottage Grove, Oregon. He married Sadie Vincheller in 1880 and raised eight children on the ranch, three of whom became doctors. He lived on the ranch until his death in 1944, two days after his ninetieth birthday.

The ranch ran cattle under the Hashknife brand, which Vandevert had used years earlier as a range foreman for the Aztec Land and Cattle Company in Arizona and Texas. The brand originated with Texas cattle camp cooks in the 1870s, cut in the shape of the knife they used to chop hash. The homestead doubled as a U.S. post office and a stagecoach stop in its early years. Nearby, the one-room Harper School, built in 1925 and moved to its current spot on the ranch in 1929, taught Vandevert children and their neighbors' kids until it closed for good in the 1950s. Both the log homestead and the schoolhouse still stand, restored, and the homeowners association's own history places them among the sites Deschutes County recognizes as historic. The family kept living on the ranch through three generations. Claude Vandevert, William's son, sold the 320 acres in 1970, though he kept the right to live out his life there with his wife.

Ownership changed hands more than once before Vandevert Ranch became a residential community. Brothers Michael and John Stone held the ranch through the early 1980s, and Jim and Carol Gardner bought it out of bankruptcy in 1987. The Gardners restored the homestead and turned the surrounding land, 400 acres in all, into a gated community, opening 21 custom homesites to buyers in 1993 under covenants that require log, timber, or stone construction. Fifteen houses stood on the ranch by 2002. Jim Gardner, a Harvard graduate and former president of Lewis and Clark College, wrote out a governing philosophy for the ranch in 1991 built around natural beauty, historic integrity, privacy, and low density, a document the homeowners association still points to today. Day-to-day management now runs through Aperion Property Management, which also manages Crosswater, Pronghorn, and the Ranch at the Canyons.

The common land carries forest, pasture, and river frontage along both banks of the Little Deschutes, centered on a stocked pond longtime owners call Rainbow Lake, plus stables, paddocks, and about 8 miles of riding trail. Elk and mule deer pass through seasonally, and otter, beaver, and osprey are common along the river. There is no golf course on the ranch itself. Riders, canoeists, anglers, and golfers headed to the neighboring Crosswater Golf Course can do all four within a mile of their own front door, according to the homeowners association. Kids on the ranch fall inside the Bend-La Pine School District, which also covers Sunriver and the Three Rivers corridor along US-97, worth confirming directly for a specific address. Most owners, by the association's own account, treat the ranch as a second home rather than a full-time address.

The trade-off is the one that comes with any home built inside pine forest 15 miles from town. Living here means clearing brush and keeping defensible space, not just landscaping. The ranch's own Natural Resources Stewardship Plan includes a wildfire risk map prepared under Oregon's Senate Bill 360 forestland-urban interface standards, a planning requirement most Bend subdivisions never face. Deschutes County treated the wider area as enough of a wildfire priority to win a $3.4 million federal Community Wildfire Defense Grant in 2025 for mitigation work across south county. None of that makes the ranch unsafe. It does mean fire-season vigilance and a longer drive for groceries, medical care, and daily errands than a subdivision inside Bend's city limits requires. For the privacy, the river frontage, and a pace that still runs more like a ranch than a neighborhood, the owners who buy here have made that trade on purpose.

amenities.name: Little Deschutes River Access
amenities.description: Private put-in and take-out points run along both banks of the river through the property.

amenities.name: Private Fishing Pond
amenities.description: A 3.2-acre pond with 1,000 feet of shoreline, stocked with rainbow trout.

amenities.name: Equestrian Facilities
amenities.description: Horse boarding with stables, a riding arena, paddocks, pasture, and 8 miles of riding trails, with a full-time animal caretaker.

amenities.name: Tennis and Pickleball Courts
amenities.description: On-site courts for community residents, alongside walking and biking trails through the common land.

amenities.name: Historic Homestead and Schoolhouse
amenities.description: The 1892 log homestead and one-room schoolhouse are preserved on the property and listed among the county's Historic Resources.

drive_times.note: Vandevert Road is about 3 miles south of the Sunriver exit on US-97

sources.publisher: Vandevert Ranch Homeowners Association (official title chronology, sourced to Deschutes County Abstract Company records)
sources.supports: Claude Vandevert sold the 320-acre ranch in 1970 to Leonard Lundgren while retaining a life estate; the ranch passed to brothers Michael and John Stone in the early 1980s before Jim and Carol Gardner bought it out of bankruptcy in 1987; the 400 acres were assembled from three original land blocks.
William Plutarch Vandevert born 1854 near Cottage Grove, Oregon, died 1944; married Sadie Vincheller in 1880; eight children, three of whom (Clint, George, Arthur) became doctors.

The Hashknife cattle brand originated with Texas cattle-camp cooks in the 1870s near Weatherford, Texas, and was used by William Vandevert as a range foreman for the Aztec Land and Cattle Company in Arizona and Texas before he founded the ranch.

The one-room Harper School was built in 1925, moved to its current site on the ranch in 1929, closed around 1936, reopened in 1946, and closed for good roughly a decade later; restored in the early 1990s.
Elevation runs from 4,160 feet near the river to 4,180 feet at the main entrance gate; the common land includes forest, pasture, and riparian frontage along the Little Deschutes River.
The stocked fishing pond is known to owners as Rainbow Lake; elk, mule deer, otter, beaver, and osprey are regularly present on the ranch.
Owners can ride, canoe, fish, and golf within a mile of home; golf is off-property at the neighboring Crosswater Golf Course, site of the annual Vandevert Scramble.

Day-to-day management is provided by Aperion Property Management, which also manages Crosswater, Pronghorn, and the Ranch at the Canyons; most owners have used the ranch as a second home rather than a full-time residence.
The ranch is about 15 miles south of Bend and roughly 2 miles from Sunriver by road.
The ranch's own Natural Resources Stewardship Plan includes an Oregon Department of Forestry SB 360 wildfire risk map and forestland-urban interface standards among its governing reference documents.

source: about_prose rewritten 2026-08-03 as long-form editorial per docs/audits/PROFILE_CONSISTENCY_2026-08-03.md and the 2026-08-02 website audit's finding that long-form editorial about named places outperforms data-only pages in search. Every claim traces to the 'sources' array above, primarily vandevertranch.org (the Vandevert Ranch Homeowners Association's own history pages, authored by local historian Ted Haynes and Vandevert family descendant Grace Vandevert McNellis), cross-checked against Wikipedia, Deschutes County, and Oregon SB 360 wildfire-law reference material. No market figures, prices, or percentages included by design; live market data renders separately from the database. Two factual conflicts in the source material were resolved and are worth flagging: the association's own history.html page states the Gardners bought the ranch in 1988, while its own modern.html and title_history.html pages both give 1987 with a documented title chain; this prose uses 1987. Secondary sources (Wikipedia, real estate blogs) describe a 22-lot community, while the association's own modern.html gives 21 lots sold plus 15 houses built by 2002; this prose uses the association's own count of 21.
